newsitem.title: USA: US CORPORATE BONDS-Grand Union extends decline.
newsitem.headline: US CORPORATE BONDS-Grand Union extends decline.

text.p: Corporate bonds ended a dull session mostly unchanged with only a handful of issues hitting the market; however, Grand Union debt continued to decline, traders said.
Grand Union 12 percent paper dropped another 6-1/2 points to close at a 56 bid, traders said.
"The bonds have continued to weaken on concerns that cash flows will be lower; and that the September interest payment may be in question," said one high-yield player.
The bonds have seen a steep decline in the last two months when they traded in the high 80's area, players said.

News of a company restruturing, leading to 80 layoffs at its Wayne, New Jersey headquarters, huge year-end and fourth quarter losses and credit rating downgrades, have pressured the bonds lower, players said.
Grand Union senior unsecured debt is rated CCC by Standard & Poor's and Caa by Moody's Investors Service.
In the broader junk sector, prices ended the day mostly unchanged to 1/8 higher; however, Nextel bonds gained a point, traders said.
Nextel debt due 2003 was quoted a point higher at 91 bid, bonds due 2004 were quoted 81-1/2 bid, traders said.
Columbia 10-year bonds tightened slightly by around four basis points to a bid spread of 79 basis points following the news.
"With Rick Scott out - there is more certainty that problems at Columbia can be resolved in some way," said one debt analyst.

Bondholders seemed to have shrugged off Moody's Investors Service decision to downgrade the company's debt ratings by one notch on Friday over concerns of the federal government's investigation of the company.
Among new junk issues, GCI Inc's $180 million 9.75 percent senior notes traded up immediately on the break. The bonds which priced at par were quoted at 102-1/2 bid, 103 offer, traders said.
Stater Brothers recently priced 9.0 percent bonds were quoted higher at 101-5/8 bid, 101-3/4 offer at the close.

In other news, bondholders have reacted with guarded optimism to the resignation of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp's two top officers, Richard Scott, and David Vandewater on Friday, market sources said.
"The bonds were already trading wider than virtually all other triple B's," said the analyst.
Many bondholders assume the company's senior debt will be downgraded to the triple-B from A3/A-minus level if Columbia is purchased by much smaller, Tenet Healthcare Corp.

Moody's said it may cut Columbia's ratings further and S&P already has its ratings of Columbia debt under review for a possible downgrade pending further news on the federal investigation and the merger.
Elsewhere, the secondary high-grade arena experienced another lacklustre session with spreads to U.S. Treasuries seen mostly unchanged, players said.
Activity in the secondary arena took a backseat most of the week; pushed aside by close to $5.0 billion in high-grade debt and another $3.4 billion in junk offerings, they said.
Next week promises to be a big week for new issues as several offerings are all ready queued up to come to market, players said.
Among them: Quebecor Printing's $150 million, Brunswick Corp's $200 million, Raytheon Co's $2.5 billion and at leastt 20 new high-yield offerings, players said.
